claim: Starting from the 'nerve' neuron, we crawled 60 neurons that feed it, read it, feed its readers, or fire alongside it. Each got a blind label and pre-registered tests, and every label that failed got up to two more rounds. The inputs are crisp spelling, word and concept detectors. Several readers turn out to be dense units that are on for much of the text, so no single label fits them. Beside 'nerve' sits a small family of separate emotional-tension neurons (suspense, eager anticipation, being overwhelmed, disappointment). Their own inputs are crisp too: 'can't wait to', 'can't stand', 'life span', 'answer to', 'disconnect'. Then we tried hard to break the 'nerve' label itself.
lateral_text: Four relatives of psychological 'nerve' held their labels: suspense (L7/N9782), eager anticipation (L9/N1061), feeling overwhelmed (L12/N3688), and the word 'disappointed' (L1/N4037). Each fires on its own sentences and barely on the others' or on nerve's. Zeroing any one moves the others by at most 0.03, so they are parallel jobs, not a chain. The inverse confirms it: every relative can be driven without 'nerve', 'nerve' can be driven with all of them quiet, and mixed passages drive several at once. Their shared reader (L14/N9470) reaches 0.30–0.34 without 'nerve', through the anticipation and suspense contexts. That falsified a pre-registered prediction and makes it a hub for the family. globalMOO answered five of the six questions in 2–10 evaluations each, against about 600 for differential evolution.
sources_text: Bonsai's own sentences are more predictable to it (median perplexity 40 vs 57), yet they drive the target neurons less: 66% of its 'should fire' sentences fired, against 80% for Claude's. Its near misses misfired 27% of the time, against 3%. The gap holds after removing the 146 Bonsai sentences that leaked prompt wording ('the feature detector…'): 69% vs 80% fire, 15% vs 3% false positives. Bonsai can produce text with the concept but cannot reliably write around it. Its tests therefore fail most labels on false positives (18 of 48 held, against 38). Self-generated text gets no special treatment from these neurons.
caveats: Edges come from zeroing one neuron at a time. Spread-out effects and attention paths are missed, so the web is a lower bound on connectivity.
Labels are readings by blind agents from top and band-sampled examples. A held label passed an 8 + 8 sentence test (at least 5 of 8 firing, at most 1 false positive), not a full probe.

Three neighbours are dense (above 0.1 of their max on 1.2M to 4.4M of the 6.1M corpus tokens) and a fourth, L20/N5963, is weakly dense and incoherent. An 8 + 8 test cannot hold for such units by design. Two neurons (L10/N6901, L18/N12193) still failed after three labelling rounds.
The disproof attempts used one corpus (6.1M tokens) and one annotator model. D2 annotations were blind to band, but not to the hypothesis.
Bonsai-written tests fail mostly on near misses. They measure the model's ability to write around a concept as much as the neuron's selectivity.
Every test set and prediction was committed to git before it was run. globalMOO used one model for the lateral cluster; a crashed first run was resumed on the same model rather than retrained.
disproof_text: A neuron is only as clean as its worst-explained activations, so we went looking for them. Each attempt below was written down with a prediction and a failure condition before it was run. We scanned every token of a 6.1M-token corpus and checked each strong firing for a 'nerve' word nearby. We sent 120 weak and middling contexts to a blind annotator who could not see how strongly each one fired. We searched 1,199 sentences with no 'nerve' word for the strongest possible activation. We then tested a coarser 'force / strength / strain' job and a 'predicts the word nerve' job.
disproof_verdict: The narrow label was falsified on frequency. Only 13% of strong firings sit next to a 'nerve' word. The single most common trigger is ' strong' (88 strong firings, 16% of its occurrences), followed by impact and injury words. Both of those branches pass a pre-registered test with no 'nerve' word present (AUROC 0.97 and 1.00), but they reach about half (strength) and a quarter (impact) of what psychological 'nerve' reaches. Nothing unrelated turned up. Every strong non-'nerve' firing is about physical strength or force, and the weak bands are diffuse with no theme taking a third. The meaning alone does not drive it: courage and composure without the word, sensation, and anticipation of the word all fail. Best current reading (H5): a lexical detector whose peak is the psychological word 'nerve', with reliable weaker branches for 'strong' and words for being hit or hurt. That is one family of words, not one concept. Whether that counts as monosemantic depends on whether you define features by meaning or by the vocabulary a neuron serves.
